note: The pagans made the planet a goddess and blamed her for their passions. Dante keeps part of the idea: the stars do incline people toward love, but they are instruments of God, not gods.

context: Dante's Italian adds an astronomer's detail the translation drops: Venus turns "in the third epicycle", a small circle riding on the planet's main orbit, which was how the astronomy of the time explained its looping path.

note: In Homer, the mother of the love goddess.

The boy god of love, whose arrows cause desire. In the Aeneid, Venus sends him to Carthage disguised as Aeneas's young son. The queen takes the child on her lap, and he fills her with love for Aeneas.
Venus is never far from the sun in the sky. It appears either as the evening star, following the sun down, or as the morning star, rising ahead of it.

context: Dante never feels himself rise from one heaven to the next. He knows it has happened because she grows more beautiful each time.

note: The souls show as lights moving within the light of the planet. Each circles faster the more clearly it sees God, and so the more it loves.

context: The souls' circling dance begins far above, with the highest angels. They leave it to come down and greet Dante.

note: A Hebrew cry of praise, shouted by the crowd when Christ rode into Jerusalem, and sung in the Mass.
The Principalities, the order of angels that turns this heaven. Each sphere is moved by one of the nine orders, and the souls here circle in time with them.

quote: You who move the third heaven with intelligence
note: The soul quotes Dante to himself. "Voi che 'ntendendo il terzo ciel movete" is the first line of one of his own poems, addressed to these angels, which he later explained at length in his book the Convivio.

context: He never gives his name here. He describes the lands he was heir to, and says that had he lived to rule them, much evil would have been avoided.

note: A silkworm in its cocoon. From this heaven on, the souls' joy shines so brightly that Dante can no longer make out a face or form.
Charles came to Florence in 1294, when Dante was in his late twenties. The poem is the only record of their friendship, but this line and the quoted poem suggest the prince knew Dante's verse.
Provence, the land east of the lower Rhone, which his grandfather had gained by marriage.

The Kingdom of Naples, the southern end of the peninsula. Bari is on the Adriatic coast, Gaeta on the western coast, and Catona at the toe. The Tronto and the Verde are the rivers along its northern border.

quote: that land watered by the Danube
note: Hungary. Charles claimed its crown through his mother, Mary of Hungary, and was crowned, though he never ruled there. His son later did.
Dante uses its ancient name, Trinacria. Pachino and Peloro are its southeastern and northeastern capes, so the gulf between them is the east coast under Mount Etna, whose smoke darkens it.
A giant who fought the gods. The poets said Jupiter buried him under Sicily, and that Etna's fire is his breath. Charles gives the natural cause instead.

context: His grandfather. Had Sicily not been lost, it would now be ruled by Charles Martel's own children.
Father of Charles Martel's wife, Clemence. Their children joined the Guelph house of Anjou to the imperial house.

note: The Sicilian Vespers. At Easter 1282 the people of Palermo rose against the harsh rule of Charles of Anjou's French and massacred them. The revolt spread, and Sicily passed to the kings of Aragon. A grandson blames his own grandfather's misrule.

context: In 1300 he was not yet king. The warning is a prophecy written after the fact: Dante wrote these lines when Robert was on the throne.

note: As a boy Robert spent years as a hostage in Catalonia, held by the king of Aragon. The line is usually read as the poor and grasping Catalans he later brought to Naples as his officials and soldiers.
His kingdom as a ship, already loaded with trouble.
Robert is a miser born of an open-handed line. The remark prompts Dante's question, and the rest of the canto answers it.

quote: How can bitter fruit come from sweet seed?
note: Why are children so often unlike their parents? The question mattered to Dante, who held that nobility lies in a person's own character and is not inherited.
God's plan for the world is carried out through the stars and planets. As they turn, they shape what is born below, including each person's temperament and talents.
The angels who turn the heavenly spheres.
Members of an organized community. Man is by nature a creature of the city: that is the teaching of Aristotle's Politics, and a city needs people of different gifts for its different tasks.

context: His Politics and Ethics argue that people need a community, and that a community needs many trades and offices.

note: The lawgiver of ancient Athens, about 600 BC: the born legislator. The four examples are four callings.
King of Persia, who led a vast army against Greece in 480 BC: the born soldier.
The priest and king of Salem who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14): the born priest.

quote: the one who flew through air

note: The turning heavens. They stamp each person's character at birth like a seal pressed in wax, without regard to the family the child is born into. A carpenter's house may get a king's nature.
The twin brother of Jacob in Genesis, a rough hunter where Jacob was quiet. Even twins, conceived together, differ from the womb.
Romulus, the founder of Rome, worshipped under this name after his death. His real father was so obscure that so great a son was put down to the god Mars.
A person's gifts do badly in the wrong circumstances, like a seed sown in the wrong soil.

quote: the one born to wear a sword
note: Commentators have often seen Charles's own brothers here: Louis, who gave up his claim to the throne to become a Franciscan friar and a bishop, and Robert, the king who wrote sermons.
